Yeah, some of them some of them have had some success, but ultimately like uh you know, I ended up looking for different jobs and I did end up working at uh companies like Square and then eventually I found myself at GitHub, which is where I was right before this.
And so GitHub is obviously like a developer tool tooling place. What kind of work did you end up doing there?

Yeah, I did all kinds of things at GitHub. I worked on uh mostly like contributor pages and developer tooling. So this is like I worked on uh the contribution graph for a bit. I worked on the merge queue implementation. I worked on uh the early versions of Codespaces. I I kind of just did everything. I really liked working there. I used to say that when so I another place I worked at in the past was I worked at Tumblr. And one thing that was really neat is I know, I'm old.

It's really neat is I would like, you know, I would maybe have a rough day at work and I would walk down the subway and I would see people like using the Tumblr app and I'd be like, okay, well that's that's pretty neat. People are using that. Or I worked at Square and I would go into businesses and see people like conducting business with with the terminal, right? And oh, that's pretty cool. Um, but you never really, it's like a different feeling to build something that you use. And GitHub was my first real experience being like, the point of this company is to make people like me have a better experience with their work. And that's just like a totally different kind of satisfaction from from me.

That's interesting. Like you you can you can imagine that like cutting both ways, right? Because it's the the cool thing about Tumblr is who uses it? Everybody uses Tumblr. Yeah, I mean not anymore. But

Well, GitHub's this nice like middle ground, right? Because it's like a lot of people use it, right? So you get you get kind of the feeling of uh you're you're benefiting the whole world in in your work. Um but also the people are mostly developers, right? So I think it's like it's a nice middle ground.
or you can live in Silicon Valley and then it feels like everyone is using it.
Everyone's like...
All of the ads in the subway are about software engineering.
Yeah, you just gotta stick to the Silicon Valley coffee shops. It'll be just like Tumblr.

Right, and now you're working on developer tools at James Street, which is like in some ways an even more focused version of that experience, right? Like, GitHub is used by many millions of people, and the tools you build at James Street are used by hundreds, a few thousand people. Yep.
Um, how like how does that feel different?

I think one difference is the the depth that you can go to and that's I think why I ended up here mostly is that you at GitHub you're building things for a lot of people but a lot of times you're building things kind of to the greatest common denominator use case, right? Like you're making things that work in all the programming languages because people use different ones. You're making things that work with uh maybe the most mainstream build systems or the most mainstream test setups. Like maybe you'll support um the most common Java testing libraries or Ruby ones because GitHub is built in Ruby. Um but maybe all of the other ones not so much. What's neat here is that we can really go deep on all of our implementations.

so we can build things that like really make some general assumptions about the way that people are working. We can assume that they're using the build system that is the build system pretty much everyone uses here. We can assume they're pretty much using OCaml and Python. And we can make assumptions about, I don't know, what code review tool they're using or how they're getting their code merged to production. That means that we can make things work better and be more seamless for people.
Right, so essentially you can just build better end-to-end integrations because you know what are the things that people are actually using.

Is there like a downside to that of that encourage you to like lock into the particular ways things work now and if when you want to do more general things, like like I worry a little bit about a kind of like like premature concretization of the workflows?
That's an interesting question. So are you asking like when you when you start building something, do you end up stuck because of choices that were made previously?

Yeah, like like just to give like a good concrete example, almost all of almost all of our programming is in OCaml and Python, right? And there's a couple of other languages we have like another fun internal language for like a kind of big complicated modeling thing called Webs that does like, think of it as like a weird alternate universe version of Excel. But sometimes we want to do new things, right? So, you know, at some point we didn't used to use very much Python and then we started doing a lot more of it. We've recently started doing a lot more GPU programming. And like, boy, there's like a lot of different programming languages and like all the tooling around it is pretty different.

To what degree does this specialization have a downside of you can end up hyper-specializing on the particular things that we do in a way that might lead you to build things that are too inflexible so that when you want to do new things, you can kind of get tied up in having like overly supported the kind of particularity the particularities of the internal infrastructure?

Yeah, I feel like there's a balance between trying to go really deep but still trying to leave enough doors open to changes that might come in the future. Um, it's also worth saying, as you know, because you you lead the group, that we have this whole uh department called tools and compilers, which is mostly focused on uh making these developer tools. So in a way we've made decisions that um I think get us the depth but at the cost of some inflexibility, but we also have a team that kind of works to take us out of that when we need to. I think we're pretty robust.
